questions.q: What does calling `.split(' ')` on a String return, per this lesson?
options: A single new String with the spaces removed
A List<String>, breaking the original text apart wherever the separator appears -- connecting directly to the collections covered in Lesson 9
A Boolean indicating whether the String contains a space
The original String, unchanged
questions.explain: The lesson's example shows cleaned.split(' ') producing ['Jordan', 'Lee'], a List<String> -- explicitly tying this lesson's String handling back to Lesson 9's collections.

questions.q: Why does `String message = 'You have ' + orderCount + ' orders';` work even though orderCount is an Integer?
options: Because Apex automatically converts the Integer into its String representation when it's combined with a String using +
Because orderCount was secretly declared as a String all along
Because the + operator ignores non-String values entirely
Because Integer and String are actually the same type in Apex
questions.explain: The lesson explains that Apex auto-converts a non-String value to its String form specifically because a String is present somewhere in the + expression -- this is the type-conversion behavior the lesson calls out as a trap to understand carefully.

questions.q: What does it mean that a String in Apex is 'immutable'?
options: A String can be changed freely at any point in a program
Once created, a String's actual content in memory never changes -- methods like toUpperCase() return a brand-new String rather than modifying the original
Strings can only be created once per program
Immutable Strings cannot be compared using .equals()
questions.explain: The lesson defines immutability precisely this way, and shows that calling original.toUpperCase() leaves 'original' unchanged while returning a separate new String holding the uppercase result.

questions.q: A beginner writes `original.toUpperCase();` on its own line and is confused that `original` is still lowercase afterward. What's the fix, per this lesson?
options: Call .toUpperCase() twice instead of once
Capture the method's return value into a variable, such as `original = original.toUpperCase();`, since the method never changes the original String in place
Use .trim() instead of .toUpperCase()
Declare original as a List<String> instead of a String
questions.explain: The lesson's fix is exactly this: because String methods return a new String rather than mutating the original, the result has to be explicitly captured by reassigning it to a variable.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend using `.equals()` instead of `==` to compare two Strings, even though Apex's `==` happens to work correctly for Strings?
options: Because .equals() runs faster than == in every case
Because == always throws an error when comparing Strings in Apex
Because reaching for .equals() out of habit is a safe, portable instinct, since Apex's == works correctly for Strings as a specific accommodation rather than a universal rule across all object types
Because .equals() is the only way to compare Strings of different lengths
questions.explain: The lesson notes Apex's == does work for String comparison as a specific accommodation, but recommends .equals() as the more broadly correct, portable habit for comparing objects for equality.
